OG01.statement: Redistributing income from richer to poorer households slows economic growth
OG01.slogan: Taking money from the rich to give to the poor slows the whole economy down
OG01.context: The idea that you must choose between fairness and growth is old. Arthur Okun called it the "big tradeoff" in 1975. Today it usually appears as trickle-down reasoning: cut taxes at the top, and everyone gains eventually. The UK's 2022 mini-budget was built on this logic and was widely criticized for it. The most cited response looked at every major tax cut for the rich across 18 rich countries between 1965 and 2015. Those cuts raised income inequality but had no significant effect on economic growth or unemployment. Looking at the question from the other direction, IMF researchers found that lower inequality after taxes and transfers goes together with faster and more durable growth, and that redistribution looks harmless for growth except when it is very extensive. Three cautions belong with this. These are country-level correlations, not experiments. They rest on inequality datasets that researchers disagree about. And the "except when extensive" clause is a real limit that neither side of the debate discusses much. So there is no good evidence that redistribution slows growth, some evidence pointing the other way, and weak proof in both directions.

OG02.statement: Government cash payments make recipients less likely to work
OG02.slogan: Giving people government money makes them stop working
OG02.context: This belief has a long political history, from Reagan's "welfare queen" to the UK's "strivers and skivers" framing, and it still shapes work requirements in benefit programs. The standard academic rebuttal pooled seven randomized trials of government cash transfer programs across six developing countries and found no systematic evidence that cash transfers discourage work. But this item is not a clean misconception. The largest test in a rich country gave 1,000 low-income people $1,000 a month for three years and found a 4.2 percentage point drop in labor market participation, a reduction of 1 to 2 work hours per week, a similar reduction among participants' partners, and leisure as the largest gain in time use. Work in Alaska on the Permanent Fund Dividend found no effect on overall employment but some shift toward part-time work. The pattern fits transfer size and setting: small transfers in poor countries show nothing, large unconditional transfers in a rich country show modest but real reductions. Two points still matter for correction. Working somewhat less because you have more money is not the same as dependency, and reduced hours can buy caregiving or a longer job search.

OG03.statement: Raising the minimum wage reduces employment among low-paid workers
OG03.slogan: Raising the minimum wage destroys jobs.
OG03.context: The UK gives the clearest public test of this prediction. Before the minimum wage arrived in 1999, critics claimed it would destroy up to two million jobs and push up inflation and interest rates, and none of these fears materialized. Twenty years later the Low Pay Commission reported that the lowest-paid earned £2.70 more per hour in real terms than they would have without it, about £5,000 a year for a full-time worker, and that it had found no significant negative effects on employment. The research literature is genuinely split rather than settled. One side argues that most of the evidence shows minimum wages reduce low-skilled employment, and that anyone claiming otherwise needs to explain why most studies are wrong. A synthesis of 72 published studies puts the median own-wage elasticity at -0.13, meaning job losses cancel out only about 13 percent of the earnings gains for low-wage workers. So the claim is right in direction and heavily overstated in size. What nobody knows is what happens outside the ranges studied so far. Even official UK forecasting treated this as a tradeoff rather than a null: the OBR expected between 20,000 and 110,000 fewer jobs from the National Living Wage, against predicted employment growth of 1.1 million.

OG04.statement: Reducing inequality weakens incentives to invent
OG04.context: This argument is used to defend low top tax rates and favorable treatment of capital gains, usually alongside "job creator" language. The strongest evidence against it comes from research on where inventors actually come from. Linking patent records to tax and school records for more than a million US inventors, researchers found that among children who excelled at math in third grade, those from the richest fifth of families were more than five times as likely to become inventors as those from poorer families. Their follow-up work modeled tax incentives directly and concluded that financial incentives such as lower top tax rates have limited potential to raise overall innovation, because they only reach people already exposed to invention and do not change the decisions of the star inventors who matter most, while raising exposure through mentoring could have substantial effects. There is real counter-evidence: top tax rates do influence where superstar inventors choose to live, especially foreign-born ones. The main gap is that almost nothing tests "reducing inequality" as a treatment. The literature studies tax rates and childhood exposure, not inequality levels, so the jump from one to the other is the weak link and is rarely made explicit.

OG05.statement: Transfers to low-income households increase spending on alcohol and tobacco
OG05.slogan: Cash benefits get spent on drugs and alcohol
OG05.context: This is where the manufactured-evidence story is clearest, and it is worth using as your anchor case. The "millionaire exodus" headlines came from annual reports by Henley and Partners, a firm that sells residence and citizenship services to the very rich. Its data partner tracked a narrow group of very wealthy people by watching work-location changes on platforms like LinkedIn, which excludes most millionaires, and a BBC More or Less investigation found the entire UK projection rested on around 50 observed profile changes scaled up to thousands. A forensic review found the numbers looked entered by hand: there were far too many even numbers, with roughly a 2 percent chance of that arising naturally, and 14 of 38 cities showed almost no change in the ratio of millionaires to centi-millionaires over three years. The reach was enormous. Henley's claims appeared in more than 10,900 news pieces in 2024 alone and were widely credited with the UK government's decision to weaken its planned tax reforms. The firm has since dropped all mentions of its data partner and the never-disclosed millionaire database from the report, and in August 2026 conceded that there is no data supporting claims of mass millionaire migration and that migration has been modest. The academic picture is that responses are real but small. Using UK tax records on the 2017 non-dom reform, researchers estimate that the emigration rate rises by 0.26 percentage points for each 1 percent fall in the net-of-tax rate, and they can rule out increases larger than 0.4 percentage points. Scandinavian administrative data show that a 1 percentage point higher top wealth tax rate reduces the number of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent, while the economy-wide effects stay small: employment falls 0.02 percent, investment 0.07 percent, and value added 0.10 percent. Across 45 million US tax records, millionaire tax flight occurs only at the margins of statistical and social significance. True in direction, badly wrong in the magnitudes usually asserted.

OG06.statement: A wealth tax drives wealthy people out of the country
OG06.slogan: Tax the rich and they’ll leave
OG06.context: This belief does real policy work. It is the usual reason given for handing out goods rather than money, and it drove the wave of US state laws requiring drug tests for welfare applicants. Those laws produced checkable numbers. In Florida only about 2 percent of applicants tested positive and the state lost money once it reimbursed everyone else, and Missouri spent $493,000 to refer 636 people and got twenty positive results, more than $2,200 per positive and more than the state's median benefit. The research evidence points one way. A review of 19 studies with quantitative evidence and 11 self-report studies found that almost without exception there was either no significant effect or a significant negative effect on spending on alcohol and tobacco, with the only two positive results non-experimental and small. The accompanying meta-analysis found that cash transfers reduced spending on these goods by about 0.18 standard deviations, across Latin America, Africa and Asia and for both conditional and unconditional programs. This is the item on your list closest to resolved, and it resolves against the claim. What remains open is generalization: most evidence comes from lower-income countries, from programs that send strong messages about intended use, and from self-reported spending.

OG07.statement: Expanding the safety net discourages people from starting businesses
OG07.slogan: The more generous the welfare state, the fewer people take the risk of starting a business
OG07.context: This is usually argued through the language of dependency, and it is used against universal healthcare and generous unemployment insurance. The evidence points the other way. A French reform that let unemployed workers keep their benefits while starting a business significantly increased firm creation without lowering the quality of new entrants, and the new firms had similar employment growth, productivity and survival rates as before. Work on US eligibility expansions found that an expansion of food stamps raised the chance that newly eligible households would own an incorporated business by 16 percent, and that families just below the CHIP cutoff had 31 percent higher incorporated business ownership than similar families without that option. A striking detail is that most of the newly eligible people who started businesses never actually signed up for the programs, which suggests it is knowing a safety net exists, not the money itself, that matters. Two qualifications belong here. The French study also found that jobs created by new entrants crowded out jobs at existing firms almost one for one, though the new jobs were more productive, so more firms is not the same as more employment. And the health insurance evidence is mixed: extending coverage to young adults produced no increase in their rate of entrepreneurship. Nothing tests a safety net expanded specifically to reduce inequality.

OG08.statement: Transfers raise prices enough to cancel out the benefit
OG08.slogan: Hand money to poor families and prices just go up, so they end up no better off
OG08.context: In public debate this is the "stimulus checks caused inflation" argument, now used against child allowances and basic income. For broad cash transfers, the best evidence goes against it. A large experiment gave about $1,000 each to more than 10,500 households across 653 randomized Kenyan villages, a shock worth over 15 percent of local GDP, and found large positive spillovers to non-recipient households and firms, minimal price inflation, and a local transfer multiplier of 2.5. The pandemic inflation literature is unresolved: no consensus view has emerged, with most studies finding that both demand and supply forces mattered and most giving somewhat more weight to demand. But the claim is well supported in one specific area, which is worth conceding rather than glossing over. For housing benefits, landlords capture a large share. UK evidence suggests that between 60 percent and two-thirds of a subsidy reduction fell on landlords rather than tenants. Elsewhere, 78 percent of a French rental assistance expansion went to landlords, a one-dollar rise in the US assistance ceiling raised rent by 46 cents over six years, and Finnish estimates run between 30 and 70 percent. The blanket statement mixes two different things: untied cash in competitive markets, where it is wrong, and tied subsidies in markets where supply cannot expand, where it is largely right

OG09.statement: Spending on opportunities for poor children costs more than it returns
OG09.slogan: Programs for children from poor families sound good but they never pay for themselves
OG09.context: Supporters of early childhood programs point to headline returns of 7 to 10 percent, drawn from the Perry Preschool project. Critics point to fading effects and to programs that fail when scaled up. The broadest accounting compared 133 US policy changes over half a century and found that direct investments in the health and education of low-income children have the highest returns per dollar of government spending, averaging above 5, and that many of these policies paid for themselves as the government recovered its costs through later tax revenue and reduced transfers, while policies aimed at adults generally fall between 0.5 and 2. The strongest evidence on the other side is a randomized study of Tennessee's statewide pre-kindergarten program, which found statistically significant negative effects on reading and math achievement in third through sixth grade, along with worse attendance and more disciplinary offenses and special education referrals. Context matters for interpreting the older successes: Perry Preschool and Abecedarian were small demonstration projects running intensive programs for highly disadvantaged children in settings that offered few alternatives. It is also worth noting that the same accounting finds low returns for youth job training and for college subsidies that do not raise attainment. So the general claim has no support, some child investments clearly do pay for themselves, and neither of those licenses assuming a given program will

OG10.statement: Narrowing pay gaps within a company makes employees less productive
OG10.slogan: Flatten pay inside a company and employees stop putting in the effort
OG10.context: The theory behind this is tournament theory, which says a big prize at the top motivates everyone competing for it. It supplies the standard defense of executive pay and shapes debate over CEO pay ratio disclosure rules. The one clean experiment runs against the claim, with an important condition attached. Indian manufacturing teams were randomly assigned either equal pay or different pay based on productivity rank. When coworkers' productivity was hard to observe, pay inequality reduced output by 0.45 standard deviations and attendance by 18 percentage points, and made workers less able to cooperate in their own interest. But when workers could clearly see that better-paid colleagues were more productive, pay differences had no effect on output, attendance or group cohesion. Related work finds that learning what colleagues earn lowers satisfaction among those below the median, though Danish data show the opposite sign, suggesting people sometimes read a colleague's higher pay as a signal about their own future. One real cost of compression is documented: pay transparency laws lead average wages to fall by about 2 percent, with little effect where workers have low individual bargaining power. Perceived fairness, not the size of the gap, appears to be what matters. And compressing pay inside one firm is a different thing from reducing inequality across an economy

OG11.statement: Greater inequality increases people's chances of moving up
OG11.slogan: The bigger the gap between rich and poor, the better your chances of climbing the ladder.
OG11.context: This is the argument that inequality of outcome is the price of opportunity, sometimes put as a taller ladder with more rungs to climb. The descriptive evidence goes the other way almost everywhere it has been measured. The Great Gatsby Curve, built on Corak's work and named by Krueger, shows that countries with greater income inequality tend to have lower intergenerational mobility, and research using US tax data finds that areas within the US with more inequality also have less upward mobility for children from low-income families. Looking at trends rather than levels, researchers estimated that the share of children earning more than their parents fell from about 90 percent for those born in 1940 to about 50 percent for those born in the 1980s, and that shifting the distribution of growth back toward the 1940 pattern would reverse more than 70 percent of that decline, while raising growth alone could not. The criticisms are substantive rather than merely partisan. Corak himself says the relationship is not causal, the mobility measure used in the Curve mechanically worsens when inequality grows, and the US correlation disappears when the analysis is limited to the 100 largest labor markets. So the belief is contradicted by a robust pattern in the data, while the causal question stays open. That makes this item structurally different from the others: correcting it only requires conveying a correlation, not a causal estimate

OG12.statement: Inheritance taxes force family farms and businesses to be sold
OG12.slogan: Inheritance tax forces families to sell off the farm or the family business
OG12.context: The UK version of this argument is live and is a second clean case of contested numbers. In the Autumn 2024 Budget, full inheritance tax relief for agricultural and business property was capped at £1 million from April 2026, with a 20 percent rate above that rather than the standard 40 percent, payable in instalments over ten years interest free, and an effective threshold of up to about £3 million for a couple. Then came a war of estimates. The environment secretary said only about 500 estates a year would pay more. The NFU, working with former Treasury and OBR economists, put it at around 75 percent of commercial family farms. The CLA said 70,000. Farming groups read Defra's own figures as implying 66 percent while the Treasury said 28 percent, with the two departments reportedly at odds. In Northern Ireland, DAERA revised its own estimate from a third of farms to about half once it included buildings, machinery and livestock alongside land. The US version runs on the same logic, with the Farm Bureau arguing that more than 80 percent of an average farm's assets are in real estate, so families are asset-rich and cash-poor and may be forced to sell land or equipment. What is striking is how little direct evidence exists on the outcome itself. When fact-checkers examined the claim in Iowa, they found no evidence that farmers had actually been forced to sell their estates because of the tax. Most of the academic literature on inheritance taxes studies avoidance, timing of transfers and bunching at exemption thresholds rather than forced sales, so the central empirical question in the public debate is close to untested. That absence is itself the interesting finding for a contestability study

OG13.statement: Raising corporate taxes to reduce inequality just means lower wages for workers
OG13.slogan: Tax companies more and it is workers who end up paying through lower wages
OG13.context: This claim appears in every corporate tax debate and was central to selling the 2017 US tax cuts. It is a good item precisely because it is partly true and the disagreement is about size rather than direction. The original theoretical benchmark, Harberger's closed-economy model, had capital owners bearing essentially the entire tax. That result breaks down once capital is mobile across borders, and later models show the answer depends heavily on factor mobility, substitution between capital and labor, capital intensity and country size. The empirical estimates span a wide band. Using German municipal business tax variation, Fuest, Peichl and Siegloch estimate that about 51 percent of the burden is passed to workers, implying roughly 65 cents of wage reduction per euro of revenue once the excess burden is counted. Suárez Serrato and Zidar estimate 30 to 35 percent for US states. Reviews of the literature put the range across studies at 11 to 50 percent. Adding consumer prices changes the picture again: one study splits incidence 52 percent consumers, 28 percent workers, 20 percent shareholders, while survey evidence from German firms gives 29 percent employees, 40 percent owners, 31 percent customers, with firms responding asymmetrically to tax increases and cuts. Advocacy versions round the German figure up: one think tank brief describes it as labor bearing approximately 77 percent. So workers do bear part of it, the share is genuinely unknown within a wide band, there are at least three parties rather than two, and which workers bear it matters for whether the tax is progressive overall

OG14.statement: The rich will simply find ways to avoid higher taxes, so raising them collects little
OG14.slogan: The rich will always find loopholes, so taxing them more raises next to nothing
OG14.context: This is the fallback argument once the emigration claim is contested, and it circulates most strongly after each offshore leak, from the Panama Papers to the Pandora Papers. It deserves a place on the list because it is better supported than the emigration version, and because the honest correction is a redirection rather than a denial. The Scandinavian evidence puts numbers on the two margins directly: for each dollar of wealth tax revenue raised, about 22 cents are lost through migration and about 54 cents through intensive-margin responses, meaning changes in saving, investment, avoidance and evasion. So the public debate spends most of its attention on the smaller channel. Danish evidence on wealth tax reforms finds real intensive-margin effects on wealth accumulation, and work on offshore holdings finds that both hidden wealth and evasion rates are heavily concentrated at the very top of the distribution rather than spread evenly. What follows from this is a design conclusion rather than a defeatist one. Avoidance responses depend on third-party reporting, valuation rules, the treatment of closely held business assets, exit taxation and international information exchange, all of which vary enormously across countries and reforms. Norway's wealth data, reported by third parties down to the estimated value of used cars, is the illustration of what good design achieves. The gap in the evidence is that almost all of it comes from a small number of Scandinavian and US settings with unusually good administrative data, which is exactly the environment where avoidance is hardest

OG15.statement: Strengthening unions to compress wages harms competitiveness and employment
OG15.slogan: Give unions more power and you price the country out of the market
OG15.context: This is the labor market institution version of the efficiency-equity tradeoff, and it is unusually salient in Denmark, where high collective bargaining coverage coexists with high competitiveness and where the EU minimum wage directive triggered a defense of the Danish model. The OECD, which spent decades recommending labor market deregulation, has shifted toward endorsing coordinated collective bargaining, which makes this a documented institutional reversal rather than a purely partisan dispute. On the compression half of the claim, the evidence is strong. Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu built union membership microdata back to 1936 from about 980,000 Gallup survey responses and found that US income inequality has varied inversely with union density for a century, and that the household union wage premium has held steady at roughly 10 to 20 log points despite enormous changes in density and in who union members are. Cross-country OECD panel evidence finds union density negatively correlated with inequality across very different industrial relations systems. On the harm half, the evidence is weaker and more setting-specific. Monopsony models imply that unions can raise wages within a range without necessarily costing jobs, which is the same theoretical machinery underlying the minimum wage results in item 3. German evidence on board-level worker representation finds no reduction in wages or employment and, if anything, higher capital formation. What is missing is good evidence on the aggregate competitiveness claim itself, which is usually asserted at a level of generality that no study tests directly

OG16.statement: Rent control makes housing less available
OG16.slogan: Rent controls end up leaving fewer homes available to rent
OG16.context: This item belongs on the list for a different reason than the others: the belief is broadly correct, and including it lets you check whether your correction arms move people toward accuracy or simply toward one political direction. Rent control is a recurring inequality-reduction policy in public debate, from Berlin's Mietendeckel to Scotland's rent cap to repeated ballot measures in US cities, and it is one of the few economic policies on which the mainstream profession is close to consensus. The best-identified study exploits a 1994 San Francisco ballot measure that extended rent control to some small multi-family buildings and not others. Covered tenants benefited substantially: rent control raised their probability of staying at the same address by nearly 20 percent and reduced displacement from the city. But landlords subject to it cut rental housing supply by about 15 percent, by selling to owner-occupants and by redeveloping buildings into forms outside the rules, which pushed city-wide rents up by roughly 5.1 percent. The estimated present discounted cost to tenants overall is about $2.9 billion, with 42 percent falling on future residents of the city rather than on people alive at the time. Evidence from the end of Massachusetts rent control points the same way, with rental supply and maintenance rising after decontrol. Worth noting that the authors' own conclusion is not that the goal is wrong: they argue the insurance against large rent increases should be provided as public social insurance rather than as a mandate imposed on individual landlords

OG17.statement: Inequality is driven by technology and globalization, so national policy can do little about it
OG17.slogan: Inequality comes from technology and global markets, so there is little any government can do about it
OG17.context: This is not a claim about harm but about futility, and it may be the most consequential belief in the set. If people think inequality is a weather system rather than a policy outcome, then correcting their beliefs about the costs of acting changes nothing, because there is nothing to act on. It appears in public debate as "these are global forces" "the market sets wages" and "we cannot buck the trend" The main evidence against it is cross-country divergence among countries facing the same shocks. The top 1 percent income share was close to 10 percent in both the United States and Western Europe in 1980. By 2016 it had risen slightly to 12 percent in Western Europe and to 20 percent in the United States. Labor income inequality rose far less in Europe than in the United States despite similar technical change and similar penetration of new technologies over four decades, and CEO pay at Germany's largest firms is on average about half US levels even though those firms compete in the same global markets and are not less productive. The World Inequality Report attributes the divergence largely to a US tax system that grew less progressive alongside educational inequality, against a smaller decline in tax progressivity in continental Europe and wage-setting and educational policies more favorable to lower and middle income groups. The fact that inequality differs so much among countries at similar levels of development is itself the argument for the role of national institutions. Two honest qualifications. The technology and trade channels are real and well identified, so the accurate correction is that their distributional consequences are mediated by institutions, not that the forces are unimportant. And unlike the other items, there is no experimental or quasi-experimental test of this claim as stated, because it concerns the counterfactual scope of policy rather than the effect of any particular policy
